everyone.title: For everyone
everyone.lede: Problems a town, an association or a whole society has, and nobody owns.

groupChat.problem: “We agreed on it in the group chat. Two weeks later, nobody agrees on what we agreed.”
groupChat.solution: Put the question to the group as a suggestion, in plain words, with exactly what would change. Members vote with one click, and the result stays on the record with every vote behind it.

nightShift.problem: “The vote is on Tuesday at seven, and I work nights.”
nightShift.solution: A vote runs for up to a week, not one evening. Vote from your phone when you have a minute, and change your vote until it closes.

loudestWins.problem: “Five ideas for one budget. A yes-or-no vote splits the room, and the loudest idea wins.”
loudestWins.solution: Choose how the votes are counted for that decision: by ranking, approval, scores or dots, not only yes or no.

noWallet.problem: “Every voting tool I try wants me to install an app or set up a wallet first.”
noWallet.solution: Sign in with your OrangeCat account and vote with one click. No wallet, no key. If you want proof that anyone can check, sign your vote with your own key instead.

startGroup.problem: “We're starting a club, and nobody knows how we should decide things.”
startGroup.solution: Start an organization in a minute and take the first seat. Choose who decides: you alone, every member, or elected delegates. Or start from ready-made rules for an association, a co-op or a company board.

moving.problem: “We might move, and we want to know what tax we would pay in each town.”
moving.solution: Put up to four Swiss places side by side and enter your taxable income. You get an estimate of the income tax in each, with the official source behind every figure. What you type stays in your browser.

closedDoors.problem: Decisions taken behind closed doors, and minutes nobody can check.
closedDoors.solution: Every suggestion, every vote cast and every result is on a public record anyone can read. It only grows: nothing on it can be edited or deleted, not even by us.

trustTheCount.problem: People stop accepting results they cannot check for themselves.
trustTheCount.solution: Each decision is published with what it takes to recount it. A vote a member signed with their own key can be checked by anyone, without trusting Solon.

algorithmDecides.problem: Software is starting to decide who gets help, and who gets in.
algorithmDecides.solution: Each group decides which questions only people may vote on. A new one starts with help for a person, who may join, safety, and the rules themselves. AI agents can be members and make suggestions, but on those questions their votes are refused.

hiddenRules.problem: People join groups without knowing who really decides.
hiddenRules.solution: Every organization on Solon states who decides in one plain sentence on its public page, next to its members: one person, every member, or elected delegates.

platformRules.problem: Platforms change the rules on their users overnight.
platformRules.solution: OrangeCat keeps two of its own rules on Solon: how much its AI agent may spend, and how revenue is shared with the people whose code it is built on. Every version is public, and a new one is recorded only after a vote has passed.

whereYouLive.problem: Few people can say which authority is responsible for what, where they live.
whereYouLive.solution: Type a Swiss postcode or a place name. Solon shows the municipality and every level above it, which of them levy tax, and the official source behind each fact.

roots.title: An open square. A public ledger. Rules anyone can fork.
roots.body: The citizens of Glarus have made their laws in the open since at least 1387: anyone may speak, anyone may propose a change. In 2009 Bitcoin showed that a public record can be checked by anyone without trusting whoever keeps it. Open-source software showed that a set of rules can be copied, changed and offered back. Solon brings the open assembly and the recountable record to any group, anywhere — and is building the third: rules you can fork, and leave with.

Security.metaDescription: Why Solon can be trusted with a group's decisions: what it refuses to hold, and what anyone can check.
Security.title: What we refuse to hold
Security.lede: Solon's security comes from what it cannot do: it holds no money, keeps no one's keys, and cannot rewrite what happened.

money.title: We never hold your money
money.body: Solon watches the accounts a group registers and shows where money went. There is no code path that can spend.
money.d1: A treasury is an address to observe — a label and an address, nothing more
money.d2: Balances are read from the public chain, not from Solon's own numbers

keys.title: We never hold anyone's keys
keys.body: Nothing on Solon's servers lets an attacker vote as someone else with a signature, or move a single coin.
keys.d1: Members who sign keep their key in their own wallet
keys.d2: Agent members (the Cat, Loki) sign on their own machines — Solon only ever sees signatures

proof.title: Every vote says what proves it
proof.body: A member votes with one click while signed in, or signs with their own key. Every vote and proposal records which.
proof.d1: A one-click vote is Solon's record of a signed-in member's choice — convenient, and it asks you to trust Solon
proof.d2: A signed vote is accepted only if it matches the member's registered key, and anyone can re-check it
proof.d3: One ballot per member per vote; voting again replaces it until the vote closes

record.title: The record only grows
record.body: Every step — a proposal, a vote opening, each ballot, the result — is written once. Nothing in the code can edit or delete it.
record.d1: The public record shows the entries themselves, not a summary of them
record.d2: The rules a vote ran under are frozen when it opens, so a later change cannot rewrite a past decision
record.d3: Every decision is published as one document with everything needed to recount it

seize.title: Nothing to seize
seize.body: Breaking into Solon's servers yields no keys and no money — only records that were already public.

forge.title: Nothing to forge
forge.body: A signed vote cannot be faked by anyone, Solon included. Groups that want that guarantee for a decision can ask members to sign.

rewrite.title: Nothing to rewrite
rewrite.body: A decision travels with its evidence. Anyone relying on it can recount it themselves — Solon's word is evidence, not authority.

deeper.p1: Solon records each resolution as a proposal with a category (policy, spending, membership…). Opening a vote freezes the rules that apply — who may vote, the threshold, the quorum — so a later change to the rules cannot reach back into a past decision.
deeper.p2: Each vote records how it was proven: one click by a signed-in director (Solon's record), or a signature with the director's own key (anyone can verify it). Solon does not replace your legal obligations: where the law requires a signed paper resolution, Solon is the record behind it, not a substitute.

deeper.p1: The town template counts yes/no questions by simple majority with a quorum, and uses ranked or approval voting when there are several options — where a simple majority can elect the option most people rank last (see the counting page).

deeper.p2: Whether a vote held on Solon satisfies your statutes and the law depends on what your statutes allow — many permit written or electronic votes, some do not. We will look at yours with you before your first real decision.

deeper.p1: The collective template favours consent decisions — a proposal passes unless someone raises a reasoned objection — which suits small groups that work closely together. As a group grows, it can move to majority or ranked voting by amending its rules.
deeper.p2: Exit matters as much as voice. Solon's record is designed so that a group, or a member, can take their signed history elsewhere and have it verified again without Solon.

networkStates.title: Governance infrastructure for a new kind of country.
networkStates.lede: A network state starts as an online community and grows toward land and recognition. Every step of that path is a governance problem. Solon is built to carry it from the first member onward.

definition.title: What a network state is
definition.quote: A network state is a highly aligned online community with a capacity for collective action that crowdfunds territory around the world and eventually gains diplomatic recognition from pre-existing states.
definition.body: Srinivasan's path runs from a startup society to a network union to a network state — "cloud first, land last, but not land never." No network state has been recognized yet. What exists today are the early stages, and they are exactly where governance decides whether a community holds together.
definition.stance: Solon does not take a side on any community's cause. It is neutral infrastructure: the same rules engine and the same open record for any group that wants to govern itself.

path.title: The path, and what each step needs

s1.needs: A founding record and a roll of members.
s1.solon: Found the organization and take the first seat; every later admission is on the record.

s2.needs: A way to decide together that members trust.
s2.solon: Proposals, votes and counting methods the community chooses — and can change by vote.

s3.step: Build trust offline and an economy online
s3.needs: Open books and money that moves without a bank.
s3.solon: Open treasuries on Solon; payments and funding through OrangeCat.

s4.needs: Pooled money spent only as the members decided.
s4.solon: Spending decided by vote, carried out through OrangeCat, receipts on the record.

s5.needs: Local groups that govern themselves and decide some things together.
s5.solon: Groups of groups: each place its own organization, all members of a larger one.

s6.needs: A membership count anyone can verify.
s6.solon: A signed roll: members who sign their seat can be counted without trusting a clerk.

s7.solon: Years of decisions anyone can recount. Recognition is political; the record is how a community earns the conversation.

deeper.p1: Srinivasan's own definition includes "a consensual government limited by a social smart contract". Solon's approach to that phrase is deliberately plain: the rules are data the members can read and amend by vote, every decision is published with the evidence to recount it, and the executors — money and work — act only on a verified decision.
deeper.p2: Two cautions carried over from history. A majority can wrongly decide who counts — Appenzell Innerrhoden's assembly refused women the vote until a federal court intervened in 1990 — so decisions about membership are reserved to people and recorded in full. And software is not sovereignty: Solon can make a community legible and accountable; it cannot make a border move.

Ideas.metaDescription: Solon stands on old ideas: public law, open assemblies, fair counting, the commons, exit and voice, and new ones like the network state.
Ideas.kicker: The art and science of governance
Ideas.title: The ideas behind Solon
Ideas.lede: Nothing here is new, and that is the point. People have been working out how to decide together for thousands of years — in town squares, in markets, and lately in public ledgers and open code. Solon is built on what they learned.

solon.title: Solon: laws anyone can read
solon.story: Solon of Athens, whose name this project borrows, reformed the laws of a city on the edge of civil war. According to ancient sources he freed Athenians who had been enslaved for debt, and he had the laws written on wooden tablets set up in public, where anyone could read them. Then he left the city for ten years, so that nobody could press him to change them.
solon.meaning: Rules must be readable by the people they bind — and the person who writes them must be bound by them too.
solon.note: Our sources on Solon are late and incomplete; historians still debate the details.

landsgemeinde.title: The Landsgemeinde: the whole community in one square
landsgemeinde.story: In Glarus, citizens have met in the open air to make their laws since at least 1387. Anyone may speak and propose a change on the day: in 2006 one citizen's amendment from the floor merged twenty-five municipalities into three, going further than the government had proposed. In 2007 Glarus became the first Swiss canton to let sixteen-year-olds vote on cantonal matters.
landsgemeinde.story2: Appenzell Innerrhoden holds its own assembly on the last Sunday of April, where men may still show a sword instead of a voting card. It is also the warning: its assembly voted down women's right to vote until 1990, when the Federal Supreme Court ruled that excluding women broke the constitution. Women first voted there in 1991.
landsgemeinde.meaning: Open assemblies work. And the first question of any group — who counts? — is too important to leave to a simple majority. On Solon, decisions about membership are for people only, and recorded in full.
landsgemeinde.caption: A Landsgemeinde in the late eighteenth century (Museum Appenzell).

counting.title: Condorcet and Arrow: the count is never neutral
counting.story: In 1785 the Marquis de Condorcet showed that a group can prefer A to B, B to C and C to A — even when every member's own preferences are perfectly consistent. In 1951 Kenneth Arrow proved that with three or more options no ranked voting rule meets a short list of reasonable fairness conditions all at once.
counting.meaning: How you count is a choice, and it changes the result. Solon offers six methods, shows what each one does, and records which one each decision used.
counting.note: Arrow's theorem concerns ranked methods; score methods fall outside its conditions. It does not mean no vote can be fair.

ledger.title: A public ledger: verify, don't trust
ledger.story: On 31 October 2008 someone writing as Satoshi Nakamoto published a nine-page paper describing electronic cash with no trusted third party. Every transaction goes into one public record that only grows; each block carries the hash of the block before it, so rewriting the past means redoing all the work done since. The network started on 3 January 2009. Nobody has to trust whoever keeps the record: anyone can check it.
ledger.meaning: A vote signed with a Bitcoin key is published with its signature, so anyone can recount a decision without trusting Solon, and every copy of a law Solon holds carries the hash of the publisher's text. Next: chain the whole record and anchor it to Bitcoin, so that nothing can be quietly left out.
ledger.note: Solon uses Bitcoin's way of signing a message; it holds no coins and no keys.

openSource.title: Rules as open source
openSource.story: In 1983 Richard Stallman announced the GNU project, and with it the idea that anyone may read, copy, change and share the rules a program follows. In 2005 git made every change to a text a recorded step that can be compared and undone, and every copy a full fork that can go its own way or be merged back. Millions of people now write rules together this way, most of whom have never met.
openSource.meaning: A law in Solon is text with a history, not a PDF: each version, what changed and the hash that proves it. Next: propose a change to any article as a redline anyone can read, and fork a group's whole rulebook into a new group.

ostrom.title: Elinor Ostrom: communities can govern their commons
ostrom.story: Elinor Ostrom studied fisheries, forests and irrigation systems that communities had run well for generations, without a state or a market taking over. She found eight design principles they shared: clear boundaries; rules fitted to local conditions; the people affected help make the rules; monitoring; graduated sanctions; ways to resolve conflict; outside recognition of the right to organize; and nested layers for larger systems.
ostrom.meaning: These principles are Solon's checklist: a clear roll of members, rules the group writes and changes itself, a public record anyone can monitor, and — still to build — graduated sanctions, dispute resolution and groups of groups.
ostrom.note: Ostrom's own warning: there are no panaceas. Principles, not a recipe.

exit.title: Exit and voice
exit.story: Albert Hirschman observed that members of a failing organization have two responses: leave (exit) or speak up (voice) — and that loyalty delays exit and gives voice time to work. Charles Tiebout modelled people choosing among local governments the way they choose among goods, an idea often summed up as voting with your feet.
exit.meaning: Voice needs a place to be heard, and exit needs to stay possible. Solon gives members a vote on the record — and is designed so a member or a whole group can leave with their history.
exit.note: Tiebout's model assumes people can move freely and at no cost; real life is harder, which is why exit has to be designed for.

panarchy.title: Panarchy and the framework for utopias
panarchy.story: In 1860 the Belgian botanist Paul-Émile de Puydt proposed that people should be able to choose their government the way they choose an insurer — without moving house. A century later the philosopher Robert Nozick described the minimal state as "a framework for utopias": a place where people form and leave communities of their own design.
panarchy.meaning: Solon takes no side on which rules are best. It is infrastructure for any rules a group chooses — consensus or majority, assembly or board.

polycentric.title: Polycentric law: more than one legal order at once
polycentric.story: For centuries, merchants across Europe settled their disputes under the law merchant, rules they made and enforced among themselves alongside the law of kings and towns. Medieval Iceland, from 930 to 1262, had courts and laws but no king and no executive, and a free man could choose which chieftain represented him and change his mind. In the 1970s Murray Rothbard and David Friedman argued that law itself could be supplied by competing providers among whom people choose.
polycentric.meaning: Solon does not decide how much government is right. A group may choose heavy coordination or almost none, a commune or a company; what Solon holds to is that the rules are public and members can leave.
polycentric.note: Historians dispute how independent the law merchant was of royal courts, and Friedman's reading of Iceland is contested too.

charterCities.title: Charter cities: new rules need trust
charterCities.story: The economist Paul Romer proposed building new cities under new charters — different rules, chosen in advance, that people could opt into by moving there. The early attempts showed how much depends on legitimacy: in Honduras he resigned from the project's transparency commission in 2012 after agreements were signed without it.
charterCities.meaning: New rules only work if the people living under them can see how they are made and enforced. Transparency is not a feature; it is the condition.

networkState.title: The network state
networkState.story: Balaji Srinivasan's The Network State describes communities that form online around a shared purpose, organize for collective action, crowdfund land around the world, and seek diplomatic recognition — cloud first, land last.
networkState.meaning: If communities are going to be founded online, they need governance from their first day: a roll, rules, a record and open books. That is what Solon is.

closing.title: What Solon takes from all of it
closing.t1: Rules anyone can read, fork, and change by vote.
closing.t2: A count the group chose, applied the same way every time.
closing.t3: A record that only grows, and anyone can check.
closing.t4: Membership decided by people, never by default.
closing.t5: The door stays open: you can leave with your history.

NewEra.metaTitle: A new era for self-government — Solon
NewEra.metaDescription: Why governing yourselves is newly possible: cryptography, open money, AI, connection, local making and energy — and what technology still cannot do.
NewEra.title: What once needed a centre, no longer does.
NewEra.lede: For most of history, a few things needed a central authority: keeping records, holding money, doing the work, connecting people, making things, producing energy. One by one they are becoming possible at the scale of a town — or of a group scattered across the world. When those functions no longer need a centre, neither does governance.

records.title: Records
records.changed: Cryptographic signatures and public ledgers let anyone check a record without trusting whoever keeps it.
records.means: A vote, a membership roll or a set of accounts can be verified by every member — not only by a clerk.
records.limit: A signature proves who decided. It cannot prove the decision was wise.

money.title: Money
money.changed: Bitcoin and the Lightning network let a group hold and move money without asking a bank.
money.means: A community can keep its treasury in the open and pay directly — through OrangeCat — only as its members decided.
money.limit: Taxes and the laws of the place you live still apply. Open money is not a way around them.

work.title: Work
work.changed: AI agents can draft, translate, summarize and check — the clerk's work that used to need an office.
work.means: A small group can run its governance properly without paid staff; Loki's agents and people carry decisions out.
work.limit: Agents propose; people decide. Some decisions — who belongs, and the rules themselves — are reserved to people.

connection.title: Connection
connection.changed: Phones and satellite internet reach almost everywhere — a mountain village, a ship, another continent.
connection.means: An assembly no longer needs everyone in one room. Members can take part from wherever they are.
connection.limit: Being able to vote is not the same as taking part. Good design still has to make participation easy.

making.title: Making
making.changed: 3D printing and small-scale manufacturing move some production closer to where people live.
making.means: Communities can make more of what they need locally — and decide together what to make.
making.limit: Most things are still made in large factories, and will be for a long time.

energy.title: Energy
energy.changed: Local solar and batteries are already common. Small modular reactors promise compact nuclear power: two are generating commercial electricity today (in Russia and China); the first Western units are under construction.
energy.means: Communities can hold more of their own energy — and will need to govern it together.
energy.limit: Small reactors are not yet proven at scale or cheap. This is a direction, not an arrival.

choose.title: Choose your rules
choose.body: If the functions no longer need a centre, the rules can be chosen by the people who live under them — as easily as joining a club, and as openly as a Landsgemeinde. Consensus or majority, assembly or board, a village or a network spread across continents: Solon provides the infrastructure, not the ideology.

cannot.title: What technology cannot do
cannot.c1: It cannot grant sovereignty. Recognition is a political fact, earned from people and governments.
cannot.c2: It does not replace the law of the place you live. Taxes owed are owed.
cannot.c3: It cannot make a decision wise — only visible, fair to count, and possible to check.
cannot.c4: It cannot make people take part. Design can make it easier; the rest is up to the group.

Platform.lede: Solon decides. OrangeCat holds and moves the money. Loki does the work. Each does one thing, and each checks the others.

solon.name: Solon
solon.body: Proposals, votes, the rules and the record. Nothing happens to the group's money or work that was not decided here.

orangecat.name: OrangeCat
orangecat.body: Wallets, payments and funding for people and groups. It moves the group's money only as a decision allowed.

loki.name: Loki
loki.body: AI agents and people who carry a decision out — and report every step back to the record.

story.title: One decision, start to finish
story.lede: A village decides to repair its roof.
story.s1: A resident proposes the repair on Solon, with the quote attached and the amount stated.
story.s2: Residents vote. The rules the village chose decide how the count works and how many must agree.
story.s3: The decision goes to OrangeCat, which pays the roofer from the village's account — exactly the amount decided, and no more.
story.s4: Loki keeps the work on track: schedules, reminders, photos of the finished roof.
story.s5: Each step reports back to Solon's record, where every resident can see it happened as decided.

today.title: What works today, and what is next
today.body: Today one account signs you into all three, and OrangeCat already checks Solon's decisions before applying one of its own spending limits. Decisions that hand a signed instruction to OrangeCat and Loki — and receive their report back — are the next step.

deeper.title: Evidence, not authority
deeper.p1: No product simply obeys another. When Solon publishes a decision, OrangeCat and Loki each re-check it themselves: the signatures, who was allowed to vote, the count, and that the content was not changed. Only then do they act. A decision is evidence they can verify, not an order they must trust.
deeper.p2: This matters when something goes wrong. If Solon's servers were compromised, a forged decision would fail those checks. If a payment happened that no decision allowed, the record would show the gap.

methods.metaDescription: Rankings and ratings of governance and freedom: who makes each, what it measures, how, and whether its data may be shown.
methods.title: How the rankings are made
methods.intro: Every index of freedom or governance is someone's choice of what to count and how to weigh it. Here each one is described the same way: who makes it, what it says it measures, how, what it is made of, and whether its data may be shown here, with the questions worth asking of it. Nothing about a publisher's method is filled in from memory: what has not been read is listed as not read.
methods.noComponents: Its parts have not been read yet.
methods.licenceTitle: May its data be shown here?
methods.unreadIntro: These are left open rather than filled in from memory.

questions.experts: Who are the experts, how many score each country, and how far do they disagree? A score from a handful of people is an opinion with a number on it.
questions.composite: Which sources does it combine, and does any of them count twice (the same survey feeding two parts)?
questions.weights: Are the weights argued for or simply chosen? A ranking that changes when the weights change says more about the weights than the countries; on Solon you can set your own.
questions.perception: Whose perception: business people, residents, experts abroad? Perception can lag or lead what actually happens.
questions.official: Do the countries count the same way? A statistic's definition and scope matter more than its decimals.
questions.coded: Is the scale written down, and would a second reader code the same text the same way?
questions.layer: Does it mix what the law says with what happens? Solon keeps those apart, so a gap between them shows instead of averaging away.
questions.inputs: Its inputs carry their own choices and licences, listed above.
questions.licence: Its figures cannot be shown here. Read them at the publisher's, and weigh them with the questions above.
questions.unread: Some of how it works has not been read yet; until it is, judge it on what is listed.

methods.forPeople: read by a person; a program cannot read this page
methods.ownIntro: Solon's dimensions keep the law, practice and results apart and code features of the law on written scales, every coding showing its article, its confidence and whether a second person has checked it.

research.title: Research with AI
research.intro: Ask a question about governance, freedom, statistics or the law. An AI reads what Solon holds (series with their definitions and quality notes, dimensions that keep the law, practice and results apart, how published rankings are made, the law itself) and writes a short report. Every figure and citation in it is checked against the sources it read before you see it; the reasoning is not, so read the sources.
research.placeholder: For example: How does Estonia's tax burden compare with Switzerland's, and what does the law say about the top rate?
research.aiLabel: Written by an AI from the sources listed. Every number and every citation was checked against them; the reasoning was not. Check it against the sources.

gaps.metaTitle: What is measured, and where it is not
gaps.metaDescription: What statistical offices collect and publish, place by place, where the same question can be answered in one country and not in another, and what would have to come with a new measure.
gaps.title: What is measured, and where it is not
gaps.intro: Statistical offices decide what to collect and what to publish, for reasons that are legal, historical, practical or political, so the same question can be answerable in one country and not in another. Here each topic is laid out the same way: what a source that was read says is collected, crossed with what, under what law, where the answer is missing, and what would have to come with a new measure so it is not misread. Solon describes and proposes; it does not rate offices or characterise people.
gaps.stance: Solon states what each office's own pages say and what was not read. A gap may be a law a country chose; a difference in a table is not an explanation. Nothing here describes an office or a group of people.
gaps.matrixIntro: One line per place and breakdown, from pages that were read. "Not read" means Solon has not looked, not that nothing is published.
gaps.detailsTitle: The detail, and where it was read
gaps.gapNote: A difference between places is a question, not a fault. Where a law bars a category, changing it is a decision for that country's lawmakers; what Solon can do is lay out what would be gained, what would be risked, and what would have to come with it.
gaps.companionsTitle: What would have to come with it
gaps.companionsIntro: A breakdown without these invites misreading. These are what would let an explanation be tested, not only a difference shown.
gaps.risksIntro: The risks of collecting and publishing are real, and the offices that publish today have answers to them; both are set out.
gaps.decides: Whether a country collects or publishes a measure is for its lawmakers and its office, within its constitution. A group on Solon can adopt a position, or ask an office for a measure, by proposal.
gaps.proposeBody: We ask our statistical office to consider the measure described at {url}, with the companions and safeguards listed there.

why.metaTitle: Why laws and numbers, for each place
why.metaDescription: Why Solon keeps each place's law beside its statistics, marks what is not measured and shows every source, so people can decide together.
why.title: Laws and numbers, for each place
why.intro: A place's law says how it is governed. Its statistics say how it is doing. Solon keeps both side by side for each place it can read and marks what a place does not measure. It is working towards showing which measures and which policies other places used for the same problem, so that people can decide together what to change.

why.title: Why both
why.body: The law alone shows intentions; numbers alone show results with no cause beside them. Together, a change in the law can be set beside what followed, and one place's choices beside another's. Each is kept as its publisher published it, with the source one click away.

gaps.title: What is measured, and what is not
gaps.body: Statistical offices choose what to collect, for legal, historical, practical or political reasons, so a question one country can answer from its own figures another cannot. Solon lays out who publishes what, crossed with what and under what law, and what would have to come with a new measure so that it is not misread. It does not rate offices or describe groups of people.
gaps.sources: For example, <denmark>Statistics Denmark</denmark> publishes how many people were found guilty of crimes, by country of origin, sex and age, with figures from 2000 to 2025; France's <france>Constitutional Council</france> has decided that studies may not rest on ethnic origin or race.

trends.title: Trends, and what other places did
trends.body: A series shows how a figure moved over the years. A change to the law is recorded as an event: what changed, how it came about, who voted how, and what was claimed about it, kept apart from what happened. Setting the two side by side, across places, is what lets a group see what others tried.

groupMeasures.body: A group chooses which measures count and how much, as a policy its members vote on.

example.title: South Ossetia
example.status: South Ossetia governs itself and is not a member of the United Nations. Georgia regards it as part of its territory. Solon records both and does not say which is right.
example.why: Few publishers outside it cover it, so most of what can be known comes from its own authorities, and Solon records it as their account. It shows what Solon does where the record is thin: keep what is published, say whose it is, and mark what is missing.
example.sources: Georgia's <geostat>statistics office</geostat> states that, from 1994, its figures do not cover the territory, which it calls the Tskhinvali region. South Ossetia's own <ugosstat>statistics office</ugosstat> publishes a compendium every year and every quarter; the 2025 edition was posted on 24 June 2026.

law.name: Its law
law.body: The acts its Parliament and its President publish, each with the publisher's own date. The publisher does not state whether an act is still in force, and Solon says so.

budget.name: Its state budget
budget.body: The 2023 budget as the law on its execution states it, placed on the international classification so that it can be compared: about four-fifths of the revenue came from the Russian Federation.

statistics.name: Its statistics office's figures
statistics.body: Population, registered crime, GDP and the state budget, read from the 2025 compendium with the office's own caveats: the population is an estimate carried forward from its own 2015 census, and GDP an approximation, because the office says it lacks the data to calculate it fully.

gaps.name: What it does not measure
gaps.body: In the 2025 compendium, people found to have committed offences are counted by sex, age and occupation, not by citizenship, birthplace or origin, the breakdown Denmark publishes. Georgia's statistics office publishes no count of the population, and no other count from outside the territory was found.

next.name: What would come next
next.body: A page for South Ossetia listing these gaps, the comparable places that measure them, the office responsible, and what would have to come with a new measure (age and sex always, small counts left out), as a proposal people there can take up.

example.note: Researched, not yet loaded: the figures and gaps above were read from the publisher and written down, with every address and day, in Solon's <note>research note</note>. They are not on Solon's pages yet.

honest.title: How Solon keeps itself honest
honest.body: Figures are kept as published, with the day they were read; a revision is added, never written over. “Not read” means Solon has not looked, not that nothing exists. Rankings made by others are described, not used as verdicts. An AI may explain a page, but only from the facts listed on it, and its answer is checked against them before you see it.

decide.title: So that people can decide together
decide.body: None of this tells anyone what to do. On Solon a group can choose its own measures and weights by vote, ask a statistics office for a measure by proposal, and propose a change to a law beside the numbers that prompted it.
